items.text: Decision (2026-11-03): Scheduler.run_pending runs all due jobs when one raises, collects the exceptions, and re-raises the FIRST one after the loop. Errors must not be swallowed or only logged, because the supervisor restarts the worker and pages someone on crash. Previously a job exception propagated out of run_pending, so other due jobs in that tick never ran. Implemented later on 2026-11-03 (uncommitted in the working tree): each job runs in try/except Exception, logged with logger.exception, first error re-raised after all due jobs are attempted, docstring updated; TestRunPendingErrors added in test_schedule.py (two failing jobs plus one good job; checks all run and the first error is raised); full suite passes (82 tests). Alternatives considered and not chosen: reschedule-only, opt-in per job/scheduler, error callback.

Tests make time-dependent scheduling deterministic via a datetime-patching helper, first a decorator and then switched (September 2013) to a 'with' context manager (mock_datetime), with tests refactored to use it.

The at_time/at() scheduling evolved over time: in 2013 jobs with at_time run on the first day, minutes can be set when the unit is hours, and jobs run in the current hour if applicable; in January 2019 at() gained 1-second-precision timestamps, recurring sub-minute tasks like every().minute.at(':30'), and a fix for at(':SS'). Shortly after (6-7 January 2019), Nathan Wailes made at() strict: format is validated based on the selected units, an exception is raised if at() isn't given a string in the right format, and whitespace in the string is disallowed. The two-colon every().minute.at('::SS') syntax was removed (superseding the earlier form) and READMEs updated. Follow-up cleanup included docstring updates, readability refactoring, removal of unnecessary tests, line length kept below 80, .idea/ ignored, and Nathan Wailes added to authors; ConnorSkees added assertion error messages on 2019-01-12.
